correctness.rationale: For the explicit 54-vertex incidence graph, a lexicographic exhaustive iterator tests all 3,162,510 five-vertex sets (none succeeds) and all 25,827,165 six-vertex sets; monotonicity excludes smaller power-dominating sets. Two independent C++ algorithms, one from incidence coordinates and one from the published LCF graph, each recover exactly 880,632 optimum six-sets and the identical 18-cell point-count/time spectrum. Both enumerate every token slide, find 3,412,368 edges and one connected component with the stated degree distribution. A separate Python script checks the graph isomorphism and constructs two disjoint 1,296-element automorphism orbits that exhaust all 2,592 maximal-delay sets. The finite exhaustive code and recurrence are in this package; no infinite proof is claimed.

value.rationale: The smallest cubic semisymmetric graph is a canonical test of how two noninterchangeable vertex classes affect graph monitoring and reconfiguration. The exact optimum count, connectedness of its large minimum-state slide graph, and 5–10-round time spectrum distinguish sensor number, placement type and monitoring delay. The two sharply characterized slowest orbits are an interpretable symmetry-level bottleneck. These specific previously unavailable invariants are reproducible benchmarks for finite graph monitoring algorithms, not an arbitrary graph-label slice or a numerical gain without conceptual motivation.
